title: The French Textile Eco-Score: 2026 - Key Updates for Fashion Brands

The French Eco-Score, now officially called the “Environmental Cost” (coût environnemental), gives clothing sold in France a single environmental score in “impact points”: the higher the score, the bigger the impact. Scores are calculated with[Ecobalyse](https://ecobalyse.beta.gouv.fr/) , the French government’s official calculator.


The scheme entered into force in October 2025, when brands could start declaring their scores voluntarily. A second phase began in October 2026: since then, any third party, from comparison platforms to private citizens, can publicly declare the Environmental Cost of a brand’s products without its approval. Citizens have already[declared 13 products](https://affichage-environnemental.ecobalyse.beta.gouv.fr/stats) .


Without the brand’s primary data, third parties rely on Ecobalyse’s conservative defaults, which usually give a higher (worse) score. A brand’s own declaration replaces it. That's why more and more brands are declaring their own scores: the[Ecobalyse portal](https://affichage-environnemental.ecobalyse.beta.gouv.fr/stats) now lists more than 120,000 product references from around 200 brands.

#### TL;DR


-


What:


French Eco-Score, part of the 2021 Climate and Resilience Law. Assigns a single environmental score (Environmental Cost) to textile products sold in France.


- Who:


Applies to all producers, importers, and distributors placing textile products on the French market, regardless of country of origin.


- When:


Voluntary display started on October 1, 2025. Since October 1, 2026, any third party can declare a product's score without the brand's approval. Displaying the Environmental Cost is mandatory whenever another environmental score is shown.


## What Is the French Textile Eco-Score (Environmental Cost)?


The French “Environmental Cost” (French: coût environnemental) is part of France’s environmental labeling scheme for textiles (French: affichage environnemental), introduced by the 2021 Climate and Resilience Law.


It is a methodology developed by the French government, coordinated with ADEME (French Agency for Ecological Transition), that assigns a single score in impact points to the environmental impacts of textile products sold in France.


The method is based on[life cycle assessment](https://www.carbonfact.com/blog/knowledge/lca-fashion-textile) (LCA) and evaluates 16 environmental indicators. Each indicator is normalized and weighted according to the official methodology.


The weighted results are summed and adjusted for durability. Points for microfiber release and textile exports outside the EU are then added to produce the final score. The higher the score, the bigger the product’s environmental impact.


France is not alone. See how[Italy's textile Eco-Score scheme](https://www.carbonfact.com/blog/policy/italian-eco-score) compares, or browse[our textile regulations navigator by region](https://www.carbonfact.com/textile-regulations-hub) .
